observation: Opened this actual durable PNG individually at original resolution before any D015 drawing. Inventory is author evidence, not an independent review.
sourceFacts: One schematic tensile stress-strain graph. Upward stress axis, rightward strain axis, origin printed as a zero/O-like glyph. No numerical ticks, unit scale, measured strain coordinates, or ruled rectangular lattice.

Named curve points appear in the order O, A, B, C, D, E, K. OA is steep and approximately straight; AB rises nonlinearly; BC rises to C; CD is nearly horizontal; DE rises to the maximum E; EK drops while strain increases. K remains well above zero stress.
A is above Q on the strain axis; K is above P. E has a separate unlabelled vertical projection to the axis. These are three solid vertical guides, not an unloading trajectory.
Three solid horizontal stress guides terminate at A, B and E. The guide through B is below the C-D plateau; it must not be moved up to C.
The three stress-guide subscripts visually resemble the historical Cyrillic proportional/elastic/ultimate abbreviations. Preserve their roles with ordinary English labels, not Cyrillic glyphs.
All curve pieces, axes and guides are solid in the source. No dashed extension, extra curve, failure-to-zero segment, quantitative coordinate, or point F is printed.
The source caption is Figure 88, outside the cropped graph.
modernAdditions: Clean drawing-space coordinates and smooth curve interpolation express the source order and shape only; they are explicitly not physical quantitative readings.
English Stress, Strain, Prop., Elastic and Ultimate label the same source roles. Point labels O/A/B/C/D/E/K/Q/P are retained.
A schematic note may identify the nonquantitative graph. It must not introduce extra measured values.
scienceConstraints: Bind engineering stress to force divided by the initial cross-sectional area, not the instantaneous neck area.
The terminal engineering-stress drop must not be presented as intrinsic material stress softening alone. Necking/localized deformation and loss of load capacity matter; no true-stress curve is drawn.
Do not turn the source's qualitative spacing or its elastic/proportional-limit discussion into numerical coordinates or a universal material law.
